title: Barbara Allen
recordingNote: Her recording 'Barbry Ellen', released as official Smithsonian Folkways audio on the compilation Classic Mountain Songs (2002)
context: "Barbara Allen" is the most widely collected of all English-language folk ballads: the Vaughan Williams Memorial Library counts around 500 traditional recordings. The earliest is a 1907 wax cylinder made by Percy Grainger of the Lincolnshire singer Joseph Taylor. Jean Ritchie grew up singing in Viper, Kentucky, a tradition-bearer from an Appalachian family of singers, and her version keeps the ballad's plain, unadorned shape — a doomed young man, a hard-hearted woman, a letter read too late.
listenFor: The way Ritchie slows and holds the final line of each verse, a classic ballad-singer's trick before the story turns.

title: Goodnight, Irene
recordingNote: Official audio from the 2015 box set Lead Belly: The Smithsonian Folkways Collection
context: John Lomax first recorded Lead Belly singing "Irene" on a 1933 prison visit to Angola, Louisiana. Lead Belly said he learned the refrain from his uncle Terrill and may have sung it as a lullaby as early as 1908; it was published in 1936 as a joint Ledbetter–Lomax song. A year after his death in 1949, the Weavers' version topped the US charts for weeks, and Pete Seeger called it Lead Belly's theme song.
listenFor: The 12-string guitar rolling underneath a gentle 3/4 waltz beat.

title: This Land Is Your Land
recordingNote: Official Smithsonian Folkways upload from the 1997 collection The Asch Recordings, Vol. 1 (recordings made in the mid-1940s)
context: Guthrie wrote the words on 23 February 1940 in a New York hotel room, in irritated response to Kate Smith's "God Bless America" on the radio. The melody comes from the Carter Family's "When the World's on Fire". His April 1944 recording — the earliest known — includes the "private property" verse often left out of schoolbooks. In 2002 the Library of Congress added the song to the National Recording Registry.
listenFor: The tune is the Carter Family's "When the World's on Fire" — hear how little Guthrie changes it.

title: Wellerman
recordingNote: His 2021 single, the official NathanEvansVEVO visualiser upload
context: The "wellermen" were supply boats run by the Weller brothers, who set up a whaling station at Otago Heads, New Zealand, in 1831 and sold provisions to whalers. The song of the whaler waiting on "sugar and tea and rum" surfaced in print in New Zealand only in the 1970s, but in late 2020 a TikTok post by Scottish singer Nathan Evans turned it into a global hit and set off a sea-shanty craze.
listenFor: The call-and-response build, with stacked voices answering each line of the verse.

title: Seven Drunken Nights
recordingNote: Live at the Celtic Folk Festival Vienna, 1980, from the band's official YouTube channel
context: A version of the old song "Our Goodman" (Child 274), collected in Scotland in the 1770s: a drunkard comes home night after night to find fresh evidence of his wife's lover, and swallows each more implausible excuse. The Dubliners' 1967 single reached number 7 in the UK and number 1 in Ireland despite being kept off the air by broadcaster RTÉ for its ribald lyrics.
listenFor: The wife's excuses getting more absurd each verse — and the audience catching on before he does.

title: Elyne Road
recordingNote: Solo kora piece from his album The Mande Variations (World Circuit, 2008), official World Circuit Records audio
context: Toumani Diabaté (1965–2024) came from one of Mali's great hereditary griot families and played the 21-string kora. "Elyne Road" is an unaccompanied solo from The Mande Variations, his 2008 album of kora solos for World Circuit — no percussion, no vocals, just one instrument carrying bass line and melody at once. The official audio has drawn millions of plays and made the record a frequent gateway into West African music.
listenFor: Two hands doing entirely different jobs — a repeating bass pattern under a melody that keeps circling back.

title: Polegnala e Pschenitza (Harvest Song from Thrace)
recordingNote: From Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares, recorded by Marcel Cellier in 1975 and released on Nonesuch in 1987
context: The choir was founded in 1952 by Philip Koutev to showcase Bulgarian folk music and commission new arrangements of it. Swiss producer Marcel Cellier recorded them in 1975, and when Nonesuch issued the album in 1987 it set off worldwide interest; the follow-up volume won a 1989 Grammy for Best Traditional Folk Recording. This harvest song from Thrace is one of the album's shortest, brightest pieces.
listenFor: The deliberately wide, ringing harmonies — voices pitched just apart so they shimmer and beat against each other.

title: Llorando Se Fue
recordingNote: The original 1981 recording (from the album Canto a la mujer de mi pueblo), official KjarkasVEVO music video
context: Los Kjarkas, Bolivia's best-known Andean group, wrote and recorded this song in 1981, sung in Spanish over a slow, sad Afro-Bolivian saya rhythm and built on what Gonzalo Hermosa called a small, nostalgic Andean melody. In 1989 the French-Brazilian group Kaoma used the melody without permission for their dance hit "Lambada"; lawsuits followed, and the melody later resurfaced in hits like Jennifer Lopez's "On the Floor".
listenFor: The unhurried sway of the saya rhythm — a world away from the frantic Lambada it ended up feeding.
